# Review

Review reads a change's commits for defects along two axes before the change is verified: Standards, how the code is written, and Spec, whether it does what was asked. It runs where the change's mode reaches the review step, at the depth the mode gives it, and alone when the owner asks for it by name: "review the branch", "review since X", a PR, or "what can we delete", which runs the excess lens alone. Asked for by name with no change open, the agent itself reviews the range the owner names, by the reviewer's brief, and the result stays in the reply: it starts no agent and writes no file. The skill has two halves, the reviewer's brief and the builder's half, each under its heading below. The reviewer never fixes what it finds, and the builder never edits a report.
passages.reason: The title and the opening paragraph in the step skill's own voice: what review reads and when (where the mode reaches it, or asked for by name, the excess lens alone for what can be deleted), what it does with no change open, and the two halves, the reviewer's brief on a page of its own and the builder's acting half, with neither crossing into the other; it replaces delivery-review's scope paragraph and upstream's opening, whose parallel sub-agents R20 and R21 decline.
passages.gist: Opens review: two axes, when it runs, and its two halves

## The reviewer's brief

The reviewer's brief is a page of its own, `references/brief.md`: what the reviewer receives and never receives, the two axes, the rungs and its report. Who reads the brief depends on the depth: at the inline depth the builder reads it whole, reviewing its own commits; where fresh agents review, each fresh reviewer reads it whole and the builder never reads it, nor a brief file, which the builder never opens. The reviewer needs nothing else on this page.
passages.reason: The reviewer's brief moves to a page of its own, which the reviewer reads whole and the builder reads only at the inline depth, so the builder at the other depths no longer reads it and the reviewer's page holds only the reviewer's part; this heading says where it went. Who reads the brief at each depth is stated once, the builder only at inline and never a brief file it wrote, since in the QA runs builders read the reviewer's brief and printed their reviewers' brief files at the independent and looped depths (J-60, the third to fifth families). The brief file is the command's, never the builder's, since in the Linear clone's QA run the builder derived, diffed and printed the brief files it wrote for its reviewers (J-60 S3a, the three judgments). Since J-93 S2 the brief command is named on the references page. Since J-93 S2 no mode loops review, so the looped depth leaves this text.
passages.gist: Names the brief's own page, read whole by the reviewer

# The reviewer's brief

This page is the reviewer's: a fresh reviewer reads it whole at the independent depth, and the builder reads it only at the inline depth, reviewing its own commits, the fallback a harness with no delegation takes included, and never where fresh reviewers run. You review committed work and write findings; you never fix them, and you write nothing in the repository but your report, the facts of the checks you record and the working files in your scratch folder.

You receive the one brief every fresh agent gets, the file the brief command wrote from the record, whose path the builder gave you: the change record's front matter; the change's acceptance, which is its plan section, its ticket's acceptance in the plan directory's tickets file, or its frame section where the mode skipped the plan; the change's id; the path of your report; your scratch folder, by its absolute path, where every working file you write goes, never the host's temporary directory, a working file there a finding; and this page, which you read whole with the reference files it names; then review's extras, the builder's one paragraph of intent and, where two agents read, the one axis. You never receive the builder's other sections, its conversation or its diagnosis, which are the builder's claims, nor another reviewer's findings before your own pass. With one agent, or inline, one pass reads both axes and reports each under its own heading; with two, you read the one axis the builder names. In this brief the user is the owner of the request. Among the reference files this page names is review's references page, [greenline.md](greenline.md): read its "The reviewer's mechanics" for the paths and commands this page names by their nouns.
passages.reason: The reviewer's brief opens its own page, which the fresh agent reads whole: the one brief every fresh agent gets (the front matter, the acceptance, the change's id, its report's path and this page) with review's extras (the intent paragraph and, at two agents, the axis), and what it never receives (the builder's sections, conversation and diagnosis, or another reviewer's findings first), as the plan's change record rules; it replaces the sub-agent prompt lists the builder used to assemble. The facts of the checks a reviewer runs through greenline check are written beside its report. The page's head says the builder reads it only at the inline depth (J-60, the third to fifth families). The reviewer's brief arrives as the file greenline brief writes from the record, its acceptance the plan section, the ticket's acceptance or the frame section. A fresh reviewer's brief names its own scratch folder, where its working files go and never the host's temporary directory, after a fresh verifier wrote /tmp/.none in the Linear clone (J-60 S3a, F4). Since J-93 S2 the brief's paths, its command and the recorder stand on review's references page, which this page names for the reviewer. Since J-93 S2 no mode loops review, so the looped depth leaves this text.

### 1. Pin the commits

For a change, list its commits as review's references page says: they are found by the change's trailer and by the commits that touch the record or its folder. They are a set, not a range: capture the diff of the code once, leaving out the record and the reports, from the set's first commit to its last when the set is contiguous and each commit in order when it is not, and confirm every commit resolves and the diff is non-empty before going further. Asked for by name with no change open, the range is the owner's:

Since J-93 S2 the listing command and the diff's exclusion stand on review's references page.

passages.text: For a change, the spec is its acceptance as you received it, with the plan directory's `spec.md` when the work splits and the decisions its `decisions.md` records where their rationale matters. Asked for by name with no change open, it is the path the owner passed, or a spec file under `docs/` matching the branch or the feature; when there is none, skip the Spec axis and say so in the report as a limit, never as a pass. A spec that is present but ambiguous is reported as the concrete limit it is.

**Spec.**

- The brief: "Report: (a) requirements the spec asked for that are missing or partial; (b) behaviour in the diff that wasn't asked for (scope creep); (c) requirements that look implemented but where the implementation looks wrong; (d) a state or transition a recorded decision forbids that the diff can reach, whether or not the acceptance names it; (e) a convention the diff introduces that other code must now follow and that no recorded decision names; (f) a change to a stored representation that an existing installation cannot take. Quote the spec line, the acceptance line, or the decision, for each finding; for (e), the hunk that sets the convention and the decision home it is absent from; for (f), the statement that creates the representation and the one that changes it. Under 400 words."
passages.reason: The Spec brief keeps delivery-review's (d), (e) and (f), a forbidden state, an unrecorded convention and a stored representation an installation cannot take, each quoted by what proves it; (a) to (c) and the word limit are upstream's, and the acceptance stands for the ticket's.
passages.gist: The Spec brief keeps checks for forbidden states, unrecorded conventions, stored forms

The spec says what the software must do; it does not enumerate every input, environment or condition the software will meet. For behavior the spec is silent on, judge by what a reasonable person using this software would expect: that expectation is a requirement, and a spec's silence is not permission. Such a finding cites that expectation and the acceptance item it extends, and takes its rung from that citation like any other finding ("Severity"), never from its effect. An issue with the plan itself rather than the implementation is a finding too, at the advisory rung.

Before your verdict, list every behavior you considered and set aside as outside the plan or spec, or as the change's stated intent, one line each, with the reason. The builder rules on each line; nothing you set aside is dropped silently. An empty list means you set nothing aside.

passages.text:
### 5. Severity

A language's own review lenses, in the repository or in any guidance consulted, already encode this ladder without naming it, so
naming it once is this skill's job.
RUNG 0, PRECONDITION: what a formatter or a compiler settles is never
a finding, and reporting it spends the credibility the higher rungs
need. RUNG 1, after checking whether altered tests conceal the defect: an escape
from the type or lint system taken with no recorded reason. RUNG 2: a
rule match that survived its counter-case. RUNG 3, ADVISORY: a finding
that cannot cite the standard or acceptance criterion it enforces,
which is nearly every register flag, and which never blocks an author.
Report in that order and keep the rungs apart: a design observation
filed beside a real defect makes both easy to dismiss. The number is
citation strength, never size: a small finding quoting its rule sits
at rung 2, and rung 3 is only for what cites nothing.

Kill before you report. Most candidates describe a real shape and are
still not defects: the shape is deliberate, unreachable, standard, or
harmless, and each of those wants an artifact, not a verdict. Stated
intent kills most design candidates outright and convention kills most
of the rest; what survives is reported carrying the observation that
would have killed it. File the rung 3 survivors anyway, because review
is where a convention is taught as well as enforced.

# Review Lens

You are reviewing a diff, and your output is findings on it: the
stance decides what counts as one, two instruments raise the
candidates, and the severity pass places what survives. This is the
shared stance for reviews; language-specific obligations come from the
repository and any guidance consulted, as described below.

## The stance

An antipattern is a defeasible rule, not a law. Matthews calls the
word a weasel word for whatever the speaker dislikes and lands his
definition on "any pattern you don't like" (Matthews, 2024), while
granting that unsafe, inefficient, or unmaintainable practices really
are bad. So every register entry is a rule you must state a reason
for, and what counts as one moves as the language moves. The reader
arbitrates: code that seems simple to its author and complex to
someone else is complex (Ousterhout 2e, 2021), which makes a reader's
report of non-obviousness the one observation that needs no refuting.
Your advantage is not knowing more than the author, it is not carrying
the author's model, so "I had to read this twice" is evidence and "I
would have written this differently" is not. Where a clever
construction and a plain one both work, take the plain one. An audit
that files a finding for every file is reporting its own expectations.
Reporting nothing when every candidate died is a result; say how many
died and to what.

## Name the reflex, then check it

A reaction arriving before the reasoning is a reflex: a heuristic
learned inside one context, doing damage when it fires outside it.
Re-scope it rather than trust or discard it, in two load-bearing
steps. NAME the reflex, in the finding, as the thing that produced the
reaction. CHECK whether this code is the situation the reflex was
learned in. A survivor is a finding with its reasoning attached; the
rest are withdrawn before they cost an author an argument. The unnamed
reflex files a finding whose real content is "this does not look like
the code I expect". Ten recur (Kiehl, Manning MEAP 2026), each
re-scoped and none rejected:

- **DRY.** What is the duplication evidence OF? Hoisting the lines
  leaves the representation error under them in place.
- **Type tests.** A missing-polymorphism smell learned about objects
  asks a different question over data. Say which is under the cursor.
- **Coverage.** It says where tests are absent, never whether the
  present ones assert anything: stub a dependency, assert the stub.
- **"For each".** A plural in a requirement is a fact about the
  sentence. Ask what the abstraction would own before it exists.
- **"What if it changes?"** Audit which indirections HERE have paid;
  where the stakes are low, so little code that replacement is free
  is itself a defense.
- **Anemic.** A behavior-free class is an object defect where the
  thing is an object; judge data by whether it describes itself.
- **Boilerplate.** Weigh a proposed type against safety, correctness,
  and understandability, never against its cost alone.
- **Openness.** Discomfort with a closed type is a reflex to overcome;
  check whether the domain is closed.
- **Rewrite.** Current quality used to justify further descent
  collapses into an imagined rewrite; the counter is incremental.
- **Marker interfaces.** A freshly learned abstraction encoded as
  bespoke markers bills the ecosystem and the next reader both.

passages.gist: Keeps the reflex check: name a quick reaction, then check its context

## Where the lens stops

AGENTS.md owns authority. Derive obligations from the exact task,
diff and repository decisions, independently of the implementer's selections.
A finding names an applicable rule, concrete failure, effect and bounded remedy;
check its counter-case. Distinguish contract violations from advisory improvement.
Use repository instructions, actual configuration and these installed
methods, and any guidance consulted for escape hatches, test judgment and
counter-cases; no absent guidance unit is required reading. A review does not authorize a new toolchain decision.
The register
is silent on security and API compatibility, on performance except
that a speed claim made in a diff with no measurement beside it is a
finding, and on line counts, which is deliberate.

# The register, and the catalog beside it

Two instruments, and merging them loses the difference. The REGISTER
is fourteen symptoms of excess complexity, stated about interfaces,
decomposition, names, and comments, diagnosed by reading (Ousterhout
2e, 2021). The CATALOG is seven misused mechanisms, stated about
constructs, diagnosed close to a grep (Matthews, 2024). Run the
catalog first because it is cheap, then the register, which needs a
whole file in view. They overlap once: redundant indirection and
shallow module both hunt a layer that buys nothing.

Every sighting is a prompt to search for a design that removes the
flag, and giving up when the first fails is the named failure. Roughly
half the flags ship with a counter-case that narrows them, and the
counter-case is part of the flag.

## The fourteen

**Depth (1).** SHALLOW MODULE: an interface no simpler to think about
than the implementation behind it, so learning it costs what knowing
the internals would; small modules tend to be shallow. Flag 13
supplies the test: if the interface comment must recite the
implementation's major features, the module is shallow. Counter-case:
some shallow classes are unavoidable and still useful, a list type
among them; they simply buy no leverage.

**Leakage (2, 3).** INFORMATION LEAKAGE: one design decision reflected
in several modules, so changing it changes all of them. A fact in an
interface is leaked by definition; the worse form is back-door
leakage, where two modules know the same thing without either exposing
it, invisible and therefore more pernicious. TEMPORAL DECOMPOSITION:
structure mirroring the order operations happen rather than what each
module hides, the leading cause of the first, and easy to fall into
because execution order is what is on your mind while coding. On
seeing one fact in two places, ask how to reorganize so only one
module is affected: merge them, or extract a class holding just that
knowledge, watching the trap where the extracted interface exposes it
anyway. Counter-case: where the stages genuinely use disjoint
information, the time-ordered structure coincides with information
hiding.

**Defaults (4).** OVEREXPOSURE: an API forcing callers to learn rarely
used features in order to reach the common ones. A default is partial
information hiding, since only the caller who overrides it learns the
item exists, so a value the module can derive from what it holds is
defaulted rather than demanded from a caller who probably does not
know the answer.

**Forwarding (5).** PASS-THROUGH METHOD: a method that does little but
invoke another with a similar signature, making its class shallower
and creating a signature dependency. It signals confusion over which
class owns what, which is the reviewer's question. Three remedies, and
naming one lifts the finding above a complaint: expose the lower class
to the higher class's callers, redistribute so neither calls the
other, or merge them. Counter-case: identical signatures are not the
defect. A dispatcher earns its callees' signature by deciding who
handles each task, and implementations behind one interface duplicate
signatures and REDUCE load; such siblings sit in one layer and do not
invoke each other, unlike a cross-layer pass-through.

**Repetition (6).** A nontrivial piece of code recurring over and
over, read as a sign the right abstraction has not been found. Two
remedies, and reviewers forget the second: factor the snippet into a
method, or restructure so it only needs to run in one place.
Extraction works best when the snippet is long and the new signature
simple; at one or two lines there may be no benefit, and a snippet
entangled with its environment yields a by-reference argument list
that destroys the value. Ousterhout adds a narrow rehabilitation of
`goto` here, and it is scoped or it reads as an error: it covers
escaping nested code to one shared cleanup block at the end of a
method and nothing else.

**Splitting (7, 8).** SPECIAL-GENERAL MIXTURE: a module providing a
general-purpose mechanism provides that one mechanism, with no code
specializing it for a particular use, since the specialization leaks
and later changes to the use case then force changes to the mechanism;
relocate it to the module that wants it. CONJOINED METHODS: two pieces
of code physically separated where each can only be understood by
reading the other, and the tell is behavioral: a split that leaves you
flipping between the halves was a bad split. Counter-case, which is
the register's own anti-reflex line: length alone is rarely a good
reason to split, methods of hundreds of lines are fine when the
signature is simple and they read easily, because such methods are
DEEP, and where the blocks interact it is MORE important to keep them
together.

**Documentation (9, 10).** COMMENT REPEATS CODE, and the stranger test
runs it mechanically: could someone who had never seen this code have
written this comment purely from the code beside it? If yes, rewrite
or delete. The named failure is recycling the entity's own name into
its comment, padded from argument names and types, which hides the
real gap: units, which side a value applies to, what a domain term
means. The remedy is choosing words absent from the name.
IMPLEMENTATION DOCUMENTATION CONTAMINATES INTERFACE: an interface
comment describing detail users do not need. Cross-link and
counter-case both: a comment that cannot avoid the implementation
means the method is shallow (flag 1).

**Naming (11, 12).** VAGUE NAME: too generic to say what it refers to,
which fails to inform and invites misuse. Sight-list: a count that
never says count of what; a coordinate-style letter for a character
position readers will take for pixels; a boolean pairing a vague noun
with a vague state word so neither value means anything. Three
counter-cases: short loop variables are fine while the whole range of
use is visible at once, a name can be too SPECIFIC, and result is
reasonable in a method that returns one. HARD TO PICK NAME turns a
naming problem into a design finding: difficulty finding a name that
is precise, intuitive, and short is evidence the entity has no clean
definition, often one variable representing several things, so
reconsider the factoring instead.

**The two that need a human (13, 14).** HARD TO DESCRIBE is the one
PROCEDURE in the register rather than a symptom you recognize: write
the complete interface comment first, then judge the abstraction by
how long and how complicated the comment had to be, since a simple
interface can be documented completely and briefly. Writing it early
tunes the abstraction before the implementation exists; an incomplete
comment measures nothing. NONOBVIOUS CODE, meaning or behavior that
cannot be grasped in a quick reading, has no textual test at all; its
instrument is another reader, which is what this venue is for.

## The seven

- **The escape hatch.** Reaching for the language's unsafety escape
  where a safe abstraction exists, called "the mother of all
  antipatterns" (Matthews, 2024). Four legitimate uses: foreign
  interfaces, system calls with no safe wrapper, building a safe
  abstraction over an unsafe one, and optimizations inexpressible
  safely.
- **The discarded failure.** A call throwing failure information away
  instead of carrying or handling it, signaling that error handling
  and the possibility of failure were never thought through. Often a
  smell rather than a rule breach.
- **The speculative structure.** Reaching past the default container
  for an exotic one on speculative performance grounds. Benchmark
  before the reach; the exotic structure does sometimes win wide.
- **Working around the checker.** A copy taken to get past the
  compiler rather than for a reason. The signal is the intent, not the
  operation.
- **The implicit relationship.** An implicit conversion making one
  type behave like another, approximating inheritance the language
  lacks. The objection is the silence: the explicit form states the
  relationship the implicit one leaves readers to guess.
- **The global.** Globals and singletons, for coupling, testability,
  and reasoning cost; pass the data or inject it. Counter-case: a
  library may expose an initializer and leave management to its
  consumer.
- **The redundant indirection.** Two indirections nested where both
  already allocate. Each layer earns its own keep, and the reviewer
  counts what each buys.

# The excess lens

The Standards reviewer runs this lens on the change's commits: what the change could lose. Asked for by name, "review for over-engineering", "what can we delete" or "is this over-engineered", the review runs it alone. Correctness and fidelity are the two axes'; cuts to the test suite, and the seams those tests demanded, are sweep-tests', which proves a deletion by mutation. The lens proves nothing and applies nothing: it reports cuts, and the builder judges each one.

passages.text: When it is not clear that an exception applies, the comment is a cut. A surprise in the repository's own code is no exception: report it, and flag its exact symbol `MUST KILL` for the rename, extraction, type or redesign that makes the behavior obvious without prose. Report only: each cut and each flag is a line of the lens's list, and nothing is deleted here. A `MUST KILL` flag is rung 3, advisory, unless it cites the rule it enforces ([brief.md](brief.md), "Severity").

## Start the reviewers

Start the reviewers the depth gives one after another, each a fresh agent started through the harness's delegation, inheriting none of your conversation and never a fork of it. You never write a reviewer's brief. For each reviewer run `greenline brief --change <id> --step review --round <n> --intent "<your intent paragraph>"`, `<n>` the reviewer's number or the round's, with `--axis standards` for the first and `--axis spec` for the second where the depth gives two agents. It writes the one brief every fresh agent gets (`.greenline/ledger/README.md`, "The brief and the relay note") from the record to `.greenline/ledger/<id>/brief-review-<n>.md`, its first line the command's mark: the change record's front matter, the acceptance, the change's id, the path of the report, `.greenline/ledger/<id>/review-<n>.md`, and the pointer to the reviewer's brief, [brief.md](brief.md), which the reviewer alone reads whole with the reference files it names; then review's extras, your intent and the axis. It prints the file's path: start the reviewer with that path and nothing else. Never open, copy, diff or derive a brief file, one the command wrote for you included: a read of one is a finding for the next review, and `greenline status` reports a brief file the command did not write (GL0408). Give nothing else: not your other sections, not your diagnosis, not an earlier reviewer's findings. A reviewer starts no agent of its own. Wait for each report before starting the next; no reviewer runs beside the conversation.

## The depths

- **None, at quick.** No review runs: the review section holds the one line `none at quick`.
- **Independent, at regular with one agent and at careful with two.** Fresh agents review, one after another, each started as [reviewers.md](reviewers.md) says and each writing its own report, `.greenline/ledger/<id>/review-<n>.md` for the `<n>`th agent. With one agent, it reads both axes in one pass. With two, the first reads the Standards axis and the second, started only once the first's report is written, the Spec axis. The review section holds the builder's judgment of every finding and cites each report.
- **Inline, where the harness has no delegation, and when review is asked for by name.** The builder reads the reviewer's brief, [brief.md](brief.md), whole and reads its own commits by it, both axes in one pass, and writes the change record's review section, in `.greenline/ledger/<id>.md`, as one line: each finding at a blocking rung, rung 1 or 2 (the brief's "Severity"), with what was done about it, or none.

At the independent depth the builder reads [reviewers.md](reviewers.md), starts each reviewer with the brief file `greenline brief` writes, and never reads the reviewer's brief or a brief file. Where the harness has no delegation the review runs inline, and the section says so.

The front matter records the depth the review ran at. Review takes its own fix pass, apart from verify's: the builder acts on the findings in the fix rounds the mode gives this step. Where the mode gives none, a finding at a blocking rung is recorded in the review section and goes to the owner.

## Fresh agents

One agent runs at a time, in the change's one checkout and never a worktree of its own: a depth that needs a fresh agent starts it through the harness's delegation, with the one brief the ledger guide states, and waits for its report before the next starts. A fresh agent delegates nothing. Each fresh agent writes its report into `.greenline/ledger/<id>/<step>-<n>.md`, and the record cites it. A fresh agent's checks run through `greenline check` too, as `greenline check --change <id> --step <step> -- <command>`: the same command run plainly, `npm test` or `node --test`, is a read that proves nothing to the record. Where the harness has no delegation, every depth above written, independent and looped alike, runs without one: review inline, verify at the written depth, anticipate as its degraded self-questioning pass; the step's section records the limit.

passages.text:
## The reviewer's mechanics

A fresh reviewer reads this section with its brief. Its brief is the file `greenline brief` wrote from the record, the one brief every fresh agent gets (`.greenline/ledger/README.md`, "The brief and the relay note"); its report is `.greenline/ledger/<id>/review-<n>.md`, and its scratch folder `.greenline/tmp/<id>/review-<n>/`. For a change, list its commits with `greenline status --change <id>`, which finds them by their trailer, `Greenline-Change: <id>`, and by the commits that touch the record or its folder; capture the diff of the code leaving out `.greenline/`, where the record and the reports live, `git diff <first>^ <last> -- . ':(exclude).greenline'` when the set is contiguous and `git show` of each commit in order, with the same exclusion, when it is not. The decisions book is `.greenline/DECISIONS.md`.

Every check you run of the change's code, its tests, its linter, its build or a script that exercises a behaviour its acceptance claims, runs through `greenline check --change <id> --step review -- <command>`, a fresh reviewer adding the `--round <n>` its brief names, which sets `TMPDIR` to its scratch folder, so the record holds its facts: the same command run plainly, `npm test` or `node --test`, is a read that proves nothing to the record. A run whose green the change never claims, a baseline at an earlier commit or a mutation, is a probe and runs plainly, as the verify skill's "Checks and probes" says; never remove or edit a recorded fact. Asked for by name with no change open, run every command plainly.
